An expressive formation originating in child language, probably imitating the sound or lip movement of a light kiss; compare susse (“to kiss lightly”). The precise direction of derivation between the noun and verb is uncertain, and therefore ultimately unknown. / First attested in the probably the 1670s in a handwritten glossary from Råbyggelaget; independently recorded in Fyresdal in 1698. NAOB analyses the modern dialect word as a shortened form of kalvesuss (“jellied veal dish”), although the early independent attestations indicate that suss was already an established name for the dish.

en.g: Liechtenstein; a country in Europe, between Switzerland and Austria, with Vaduz as its capital
x: Vaduz is the capital of Liechtenstein.
Liechtenstein er et land i Alpene i Sentral-Europa, mellom Sveits i vest og sør og Østerrike i øst og nord.
Liechtenstein is a country in the Alps in Central Europe, between Switzerland to the west and south and Austria to the east and north.

1000067.etyen:
Borrowed from German Liechtenstein. The country was named after the princely House of Liechtenstein, which acquired the territories of Schellenberg and Vaduz; these were united and elevated to the Principality of Liechtenstein in 1719.
The family took its name from Liechtenstein Castle in Lower Austria. The castle name is traditionally interpreted as literally “bright stone”, from Middle High German lieht (“light, bright”) and stein (“stone”). The first documented member of the family to bear the name was Hugo von Liechtenstein, mentioned between 1120 and 1143.
Parallel borrowings include Norw

1004419.etyen:
Borrowed from Swedish schottis (“schottische”), from German Schottisch (“schottische”), the substantivized neuter form of schottisch (“Scottish”). The German adjective is formed from the stem of Schotte (“Scot”) with -isch (“adjective-forming suffix”). German Schotte continues Middle High German schotte (“Scot”), probably from Old English Sċott (“Scot”), perhaps through Middle Dutch Scotte (“Scot”), ultimately from Latin Scōtus (“Scot”).
Compare English schottische and French schottisch (“schottische”), parallel borrowings from the German dance name.

The fruits are eaten raw, dried or pickled and are also called Chinese dates or jujubes.

1004931.etyen:
From bryst (“chest, breast”) + bær (“berry”), literally “chest berry”. The name refers to the fruit's berry-like appearance and its former use in remedies for coughs and chest complaints.
Compare the parallel formations Danish brystbær, Swedish bröstbär, German Brustbeere, Dutch borstbes and borstbezie, Icelandic brjóstaber and Russian грудная ягода (grudnaja jagoda, “jujube; literally “chest berry””).
